cards.front: Recall a key point about British Values & Identity
cards.back: The five fundamental British values: democracy (government by the people through elected representatives), rule of law (everyone is equal before the law and no one is above it), individual liberty (freedom of speech, thought, association and personal autonomy), mutual respect (valuing others regardless of background), and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs.

cards.front: Recall a key point about British Values & Identity
cards.back: British identity: what does it mean to be British? Identity is complex and multi-layered - people can identify as British, English/Scottish/Welsh/Northern Irish, and with their ethnic or religious heritage simultaneously. The concept of Britishness has evolved: from empire and monarchy to multiculturalism and pluralism.

cards.front: Recall a key point about British Values & Identity
cards.back: Multiculturalism: the UK is a diverse, multi-ethnic, multi-faith society. About 14% of the UK population was born abroad; over 300 languages are spoken in London alone. The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination based on race, religion, gender, sexuality and other characteristics.

cards.front: Recall a key point about British Values & Identity
cards.back: Community cohesion: different communities living together peacefully and with shared purpose. Challenges: segregation, prejudice, extremism. The Prevent strategy aims to counter radicalisation. Community cohesion is promoted through: interfaith dialogue, shared community events, anti-discrimination law, and citizenship education itself.

cards.front: Recall a key point about British Values & Identity
cards.back: The role of the media in shaping British values: the media informs, educates and influences public opinion. A free press is a British value (individual liberty). However, media bias, misinformation and social media echo chambers can undermine tolerance and mutual respect. Ofcom regulates broadcast media; the press is self-regulated (IPSO).

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — british values & identity?
cards.back: 1. For British Values & Identity questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link British Values & Identity to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate whether British values are genuinely shared across all communities in the UK.

cards.front: Understanding British Values & Identity in British Context
cards.back: British Values & Identity is a core topic in GCSE Citizenship Studies that requires understanding of how the UK political and legal systems work, and how citizens can participate effectively. The specification requires you to know how British democracy functions, understand your rights and responsibilities as a citizen, and be able to take informed and responsible action on citizenship issues.

cards.front: British Values & Identity and UK Democratic Processes
cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. Understanding british values & identity requires knowledge of how democratic processes work: general elections (first past the post), devolved elections (additional member system for Scotland and Wales), local elections, and referendums. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and British Values & Identity
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
